claims.text: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a disordered high-entropy structure at room temperature.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially have a uniform elemental distribution at room temperature.
In situ aberration-corrected HRTEM with an integrated heating holder can investigate the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at atomic scale.
Vacuum or inert-gas conditions prevent oxidation during heating experiments.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles to elevated temperatures causes thermally activated atomic rearrangements.
Thermally activated rearrangements can produce local compositional segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Elevated-temperature heating can induce phase transitions in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Atomic rearrangement can be detected through changes in lattice spacing and image contrast.
Heating may cause ordered domains to emerge within the nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion drives local structural distortions or elemental segregation as temperature increases.
The interplay between entropic stabilization and elemental interactions drives local structural distortions or segregation during heating.
At a critical temperature, the nanoparticles will deviate from their initial uniform elemental distribution.
The elevated-temperature deviations may appear as elemental clustering or phase-boundary formation.
Observed clustering or phase-boundary formation would evidence thermodynamic contributions to thermal stability.
Kinetic barriers may slow atomic rearrangements enough to limit their observation during the experiment.
Electron-beam effects may produce structural changes that could be mistaken for thermodynamically driven changes.
Diffraction patterns can detect changes in crystallinity or phase transitions during heating.
Elemental mapping can track compositional variations during heating.
